Dispensational writers define "imminency" as an event that could happen at any time, but may not happen soon. They list texts such as Philippians 4:5, Titus 2:13, James 5:7-9 and Revelation 22:20. On the fulfilled reading, none of these texts uses the language of mere possibility. Paul says "the Lord is at hand" (Philippians 4:5). James says the coming "is at hand" and the Judge "stands at the door" (James 5:8-9). Revelation says "the time is near" (Revelation 1:3). These are statements of nearness, not of an open date. Read this way, the any-moment doctrine weakens the texts. It turns "near" into "possible but perhaps far". The fulfilled reading keeps the plain sense: the event was close for those readers.
Philippians 4:5 says "The Lord is at hand" with no "perhaps" or "if".
Compare a weather forecast. "Rain is near" and "rain could come any day this century" are not the same claim.

Pretribulational writers answer that "near" describes the next event on God's calendar. Nothing must happen first, so it is always near in that sense. Historic premillennialists and amillennialists agree the church should always be ready. But they say real signs, such as the man of lawlessness, come first (2 Thessalonians 2:3).
What did James mean when he said "the Judge stands at the door"?
Read plainly, James told his first readers that the Lord's coming was close for them. "At the door" is the same picture Jesus used for an event within that generation.

James urged patient believers to wait like a farmer waiting for the early and late rains (James 5:7). He then said the Lord's coming "is at hand" and that the Judge "stands at the door" (James 5:8-9). On the fulfilled reading, the picture is of someone already on the step, about to enter. Jesus used the same image: when you see these things, know that it is "near, at the doors" (Matthew 24:33). He then said this generation would not pass until all these things happened (Matthew 24:34). James wrote to Jewish believers who were suffering under rich oppressors (James 5:1-6). Their relief came with the judgment on Judea in AD 66-70. Read this way, the farmer picture fits: one season, not twenty centuries.
A farmer waits for the rains of one season, not of a thousand years (James 5:7).
Matthew 24:33-34 joins "at the doors" with "this generation".

Many futurists and amillennialists hold that James spoke of the final return. They say the church in every age lives with the Judge "at the door", because the end could come without warning. Some critical scholars say James simply expected the end soon and was mistaken. Most evangelical futurists reject that answer.
If the apostles were unsure about timing, how would they have said so?
They would have used words of condition, such as "if the Lord wills". The fulfilled reading notes that they used such words for travel plans, but not for the coming of the Lord.

The New Testament writers knew how to speak with caution. Paul wrote, "I will come to you shortly, if the Lord wills" (1 Corinthians 4:19). At Ephesus he said he would return "if God wills" (Acts 18:21). James taught believers to say "if the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that" (James 4:15). Yet when these same writers speak of the Lord's coming, they drop the conditions. They say it is "near", "at hand" and coming "quickly". On the fulfilled reading, this contrast matters. Writers who could easily say "perhaps" chose plain words of nearness. If they had meant "any time in the next two thousand years", they had words to say that. They did not use them.
1 Corinthians 4:19: "shortly, if the Lord wills" (a condition).
Revelation 22:20: "I come quickly" (no condition).

Futurists reply that the authors did not need conditions because the return is certain. The uncertainty is only about the date, which Jesus said no one knows (Matthew 24:36). Amillennialists add that "near" can speak of the last days as one era. That era began at the cross and runs to the end.
Does "shortly" (en tachei) describe how fast events happen, not when they begin?
Some futurists say it means "suddenly when it comes". The fulfilled reading answers that this cannot work for "near" or "at hand", which plainly describe time.

Some futurist commentators read "things which must shortly come to pass" (Revelation 1:1) as "things that will happen rapidly once they start". On the fulfilled reading, this changes a word of time into a word of manner. It might fit "quickly" on its own. But Revelation 1:3 adds "the time is near", and no one can come "near" in a sudden manner. Also, the same phrase en tachei is used for real soon events. Festus said he would go to Caesarea shortly (Acts 25:4). An angel told Peter to get up quickly (Acts 12:7). God would crush Satan under the Romans' feet shortly (Romans 16:20). One futurist writer even admits that in the Bible such actions all came about soon after the word was given. The fulfilled reading agrees with that admission.
Acts 25:4: Festus would leave "shortly", within days.
A parent says, "Clean your room quickly. I will be back soon." A child who waits a week, then cleans fast, has not obeyed.

Futurists answer that tachos can mean speed of action, and that Revelation 1:1 echoes Daniel 2:28-29 ("what shall be in the latter days"). They read it as "things that must happen" with sudden swiftness. Some amillennialists say the events began soon, at the cross and in John's day, but run to the end.
Do literal interpreters apply their own rule to the time words?
The fulfilled reading says they do not. Charles Ryrie defined literal reading as giving each word its normal meaning. But the normal meaning of "near" and "soon" is set aside in prophecy.

Charles Ryrie, a leading dispensational scholar, said his system gives every word the same meaning it has in normal use. He called this consistent literal reading the strength of dispensationalism. On the fulfilled reading, the time texts are a test of that rule. In normal speech, "near" means close, "soon" means not long, and "this generation" means people now living. Yet many futurist writers say these words carry a special sense in prophecy. Read this way, that is not a literal method at all. It holds the beasts and numbers of Revelation literally but treats the time words as flexible. The fulfilled reading claims to be more literal here. It takes the time words plainly and lets the symbols be symbols, as Revelation itself does (Revelation 1:20).
Revelation 1:20 explains that stars are angels and lampstands are churches. The book itself marks its symbols.
Matthew 26:18: "My time is at hand". Jesus was crucified within a day.

Dispensationalists reply that literal reading includes figures of speech and the author's viewpoint. They say "near" in prophecy is near from God's side of history, which is still a normal use of language. Amillennialists and postmillennialists agree that symbols matter, but often read both the time words and the visions less tightly than either side.
Does Luke 18:7-8 prove that "speedily" can mean a long delay?
No, says the fulfilled reading. In the parable the widow gets justice in her own lifetime. Jesus' point is that God will act faster than the unjust judge, not slower.

One futurist commentator argued that "speedily" (en tachei) in Luke 18:8 involves a long delay. So he said "shortly" in Revelation 1:1 can also cover centuries. On the fulfilled reading, the parable teaches the opposite. A widow keeps asking an unjust judge for justice. He gives in so she will stop troubling him (Luke 18:5). Jesus then argues from the lesser to the greater. If a bad judge acts, God will surely act for his chosen ones, and act "speedily" (Luke 18:7-8). The widow received her justice while she was alive. Read this way, the parable promises prompt vindication. It does not teach a delay of two thousand years. It fits the martyrs' cry "how long?" being answered within "a little while" (Revelation 6:10-11).
Luke 18:5: the judge acts because she keeps coming, and she is still alive to receive justice.
Revelation 6:10-11: martyrs cry "how long?" and are told to rest "a little while".

Futurists note that Luke 18:8 ends with "when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on the earth?" They say this points to a long wait that tests faith. Amillennialists read "speedily" as "suddenly and surely", and say God's justice can seem slow to people even when it is on time.
How does the New Testament use "near" and "at hand" elsewhere?
Every other use means close in time or place. The fulfilled reading uses this pattern to say the same word in prophecy should mean the same thing.

The Greek word engus ("near") and its verb are common in the Gospels. Jesus says summer is near when leaves appear (Matthew 24:32). He says, "My time is at hand" on the eve of the cross (Matthew 26:18). In the garden he says "the hour is at hand", and Judas arrives while he is still speaking (Matthew 26:45-47). John writes that the Passover was near, so Jesus went up to Jerusalem (John 2:13). The Feast of Tabernacles was near (John 7:2). Early in his ministry Jesus said his time was not yet near (John 7:6). On the fulfilled reading, none of these allows a long gap. So when the same words describe the end of the age, they should keep their meaning.
Matthew 26:46-47: "the betrayer is at hand", and Judas comes that same moment.
John 7:6 versus Matthew 26:18: "not yet near" early on, "at hand" one day before the cross.

Futurists agree on the normal meaning but argue that prophetic "near" can mean next in order, with no event standing between. Some amillennialists say the kingdom drew near in Christ's first coming. So the whole last era is "near", including the final return.
Why are "a short time" and "a little while" read literally, but "quickly" is not?
The fulfilled reading sees a double standard. Futurists keep Revelation 6:11 and 12:12 short to fit their seven-year scheme, but stretch the time words about Christ's coming.

John Walvoord read the devil's "short time" (Revelation 12:12) as no more than three and a half years. He read "the third woe comes quickly" (Revelation 11:14) as events moving fast. Robert Thomas argued that the martyrs' "little while" (Revelation 6:11) must be short. He noted that Jesus used the same phrase for a year or for days (John 7:33; John 12:35). He even said an open-ended delay would be unkind to the martyrs. On the fulfilled reading, this is exactly right, and it should be applied everywhere. If "a little while" means a short time in Revelation 6, then "shortly" in Revelation 1:1 and "quickly" in 22:12 should also mean a short time. Read this way, choosing which time words to take plainly is driven by the system, not by the text.
Revelation 6:11 and John 12:35 use the same phrase "a little while", and the second meant only days.
Revelation 11:14 "quickly" and Revelation 22:12 "quickly" are the same Greek word, tachu.

Futurists answer that once the seven-year tribulation begins, its events happen in quick order. So "short time" inside that period is literal. They say the opening and closing time words of Revelation look at the whole program from God's viewpoint. Idealists read all these phrases as describing the church age as a whole.
Is time in Revelation measured "from God's point of view"?
The fulfilled reading says nothing in Revelation tells readers to switch to a divine clock. The book was written for servants who needed to understand it (Revelation 1:1).

Some commentators say "the time is near" is seen from God's side, where a thousand years are like a day. They point to 1 John 2:18, "it is the last hour". On the fulfilled reading, that verse proves the opposite. John told his readers it was the last hour because many antichrists had already appeared. That is a sign they could see in their own day. Revelation was given "to show his servants" what must soon happen (Revelation 1:1). It was sent to seven real churches (Revelation 1:4, 11). It promised a blessing to those who read and keep it, "for the time is near" (Revelation 1:3). Read this way, the time words were meant for the human readers. A divine clock that humans cannot read would defeat the purpose of the book.
1 John 2:18: John points to visible antichrists as proof it was the last hour.
Revelation 1:4, 11: seven named cities in Asia Minor were the first readers.

Futurists answer that God speaks in human words but from his eternal view, so "near" is still true even after centuries. Amillennialists say "last hour" and "last days" name the whole age between Christ's two comings. On that view the church has lived in the last hour ever since Pentecost.
Does the temple in Revelation 11 show that the book was written before AD 70?
The fulfilled reading says yes. John measures a standing temple and calls Jerusalem "the holy city", with no hint that it had already been destroyed.

In Revelation 11:1-2 John measures the temple and its worshippers. The outer court is given to the nations, who will trample the holy city for 42 months. Some futurists say this must be a third temple to be built in the future. The fulfilled reading asks where the New Testament ever promises a rebuilt temple. It finds none. One dispensational scholar dated Matthew before AD 70 because it calls Jerusalem "the holy city" and never mentions its fall. The same reasoning fits Revelation (Revelation 11:2). The premillennial scholar J. Barton Payne also judged that the standing temple and the six kings of Revelation 17:10 suit the reign of Nero (AD 54-68). Read this way, "shortly" makes sense. The Jewish War lasted about three and a half years, from AD 66 to 70.
Matthew 4:5 and 27:53 call Jerusalem "the holy city" before its fall. Revelation 11:2 does the same.
Revelation 17:10: "five have fallen, one is". Counting from Julius Caesar or Augustus, many place the sixth king as Nero.

Most scholars date Revelation to about AD 95, under Domitian. They follow Irenaeus, who said John saw the vision near the end of Domitian's reign (Against Heresies 5.30.3). They read the temple in Revelation 11 as a symbol of God's people. Futurists see a future rebuilt temple. Idealists see the church protected while it suffers.
If "soon" means soon, was John simply wrong?
The fulfilled reading says there are only two honest options: John was mistaken, or the events came soon. It holds that the events came soon, in the judgment of AD 70.

Some evangelical scholars admit the problem. One wrote that the things which must shortly happen have taken longer than John expected. Another said the simple meaning of the time words cannot be avoided, and that the prophets always saw the future as near. On the fulfilled reading, these admissions are honest but lead to a hard place. They make the Bible's own time words false. The fulfilled reading offers another option. It argues that Revelation was written before AD 70 and that much of it describes the Jewish War, the fall of Jerusalem and the persecution under Nero. Read this way, John was not mistaken at all. The events came within the lifetime of the first readers, just as promised (Revelation 22:6).
Revelation 22:6: "These words are faithful and true ... things which must shortly be done" (KJV).
Josephus, Jewish War 6.4.5-7: the temple burned in August, AD 70.

Futurists reply that John was not mistaken because God's timescale differs from ours, and the fulfillment is still certain. Critical scholars say the early church did expect a quick end and adjusted later. Amillennialists say the events began soon, at the cross and in Roman persecution, and run to the end.
Does 2 Peter 3:8 ("one day is as a thousand years") let us stretch "soon"?
The fulfilled reading says no. Peter compares, he does not convert. The verse never tells readers to filter other time words through it.

Peter writes that with the Lord one day is "as" a thousand years, and a thousand years "as" one day (2 Peter 3:8). He is answering scoffers who said nothing ever changes (2 Peter 3:4). On the fulfilled reading, three points matter. First, Peter says "as", not "is". He describes God's patience, not a formula. Second, no text says to apply this verse to other time words. If it did, any number could be stretched or shrunk. Three days in the tomb could become three thousand years (Matthew 27:63). The thousand years of Revelation 20 could become a day. Third, Peter's own point is that God is not slow in keeping his promise (2 Peter 3:9). Read this way, the verse shows God's faithfulness, not delay.
John 2:19: "in three days I will raise it up". No one stretches this to three thousand years.
Psalms 90:4 uses a similar comparison to show human frailty, not to change prophetic dates.

Futurists and amillennialists both use 2 Peter 3:8 to explain a long delay. They say Peter was answering people who already felt the wait was long. They see God's patience as the reason for the delay (2 Peter 3:9, 15). Most do not say "soon" means "late", only that God's timing differs from human hopes.
Why was Daniel told to seal his book, but John told not to seal his?
Daniel's vision was far off, so it was sealed. John's was near, so it stayed open. The fulfilled reading sees this contrast as God's own comment on timing.

Daniel was told to shut up the words and seal the book "until the time of the end" (Daniel 12:4). Daniel wrote in the sixth century BC, so the events lay centuries ahead. John received the opposite command. "Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near" (Revelation 22:10). On the fulfilled reading, the contrast is clear. Far events were sealed. Near events were left open. If we stretch John's "near" with 2 Peter 3:8, we turn the pattern upside down. Daniel's time would seem near and John's far. Read this way, the command not to seal tells the first readers to act on the book in their own day. It was a message for them, not a code for a distant age.
Daniel 8:26: "seal up the vision, for it refers to many days from now" (paraphrase).
Revelation 22:10: "seal not ... for the time is at hand" (KJV).

Futurists answer that Revelation is unsealed because the church age is the last era before the end. The book is now fully open to readers, even if fulfillment is future. Amillennialists say the time is near because Christ has already begun his reign. The book applies to every generation.
What did God say through Ezekiel about people who said "the days are long"?
God rejected that saying. He told them the vision was not for distant times and would be fulfilled in their days. The fulfilled reading sees a warning for those who stretch near prophecies.

Ezekiel announced that "the end" was coming on the land and that the day was near (Ezekiel 7:2-7). God would "shortly" pour out his anger (Ezekiel 7:8). Ezekiel even packed baggage and acted out exile in front of the people (Ezekiel 12:3-7). Yet the people had a proverb: "The days are prolonged, and every vision fails" (Ezekiel 12:22). Others said the vision was "for many days" and "times far off" (Ezekiel 12:27). God replied that the days were at hand and none of his words would be delayed any longer (Ezekiel 12:23, 28). Jerusalem fell in 586 BC, within a few years. On the fulfilled reading, this is a clear pattern. God's "near" meant near, and the warning ended in one generation, as in AD 70.
Ezekiel 12:27-28: "none of my words will be delayed any longer" (paraphrase).
586 BC: Babylon burned the temple, within about six years of Ezekiel's warnings (from about 592 BC).

All Christian views accept that Ezekiel's near judgment came in 586 BC. Futurists say this proves God keeps his word, and that the end-time prophecies will also be kept in their time. They do not see Ezekiel's timing as a rule for all later prophecy, since some prophecies, like Daniel's, were far off.
How do other passages use "quickly" and "shortly"?
Each use means a short time. The fulfilled reading points to Genesis 41:32 and many New Testament letters, where "shortly" always came true in the speaker's lifetime.

Joseph told Pharaoh that God would "shortly" bring the seven good years and seven lean years (Genesis 41:32). The good years began at once, while Joseph was still alive (Genesis 41:46-49). In the New Testament, Paul hoped to send Timothy "shortly" (Philippians 2:19). He hoped to come to Timothy "shortly" (1 Timothy 3:14). The writer of Hebrews hoped to visit "shortly" with Timothy (Hebrews 13:23). Peter knew he must "shortly" put off his body (2 Peter 1:14). Mary rose "quickly" to meet Jesus (John 11:29). Jesus told Judas, "What you do, do quickly" (John 13:27). On the fulfilled reading, the pattern holds across the Bible. So when Revelation says "I come quickly", the reader should expect the same sense.
Genesis 41:32 and 41:47: "God will shortly bring it to pass", and the seven plentiful years began.
2 Peter 1:14: Peter's death came "shortly", in Nero's reign (by about AD 64-68).

Futurists agree on these normal uses. But they say the coming of the Lord is a special case, because Jesus himself said no one knows the day or hour (Matthew 24:36). Amillennialists say the Lord's coming is the one event that is always "near" to faith, even when centuries pass.
Does the fig tree in Matthew 24:32 point to Israel becoming a nation in 1948?
The fulfilled reading says no. Jesus gave a simple picture from nature: when leaves appear, summer is near. The text says nothing about a nation or a rebirth.

Many popular books read Matthew 24:32 as a coded sign. The fig tree is Israel, and its new leaves are the state founded on 14 May 1948. Hal Lindsey popularised this in 1970. On the fulfilled reading, the text does not say this. Jesus said, "learn the parable from the fig tree". When its branch is tender and puts out leaves, summer is near (Matthew 24:32). So when you see "all these things", know that it is near (Matthew 24:33). The things are the signs Jesus had just listed for his hearers: false messiahs, wars, persecution and armies around Jerusalem. Luke's version makes the point clear: "look at the fig tree, and all the trees" (Luke 21:29). Read this way, the tree is a seasonal clock, not a symbol of a nation.
Luke 21:29: "the fig tree, and all the trees". All trees cannot all be Israel.
14 May 1948: the State of Israel declared its independence. Lindsey once linked a generation of about 40 years to this date.

Many dispensationalists hold that the fig tree is Israel and that 1948 was the start of end-time events. Others, including many dispensational scholars, now treat the fig tree as a simple seasonal sign. They still see Israel's return as important from other texts, such as Ezekiel 36-37. Amillennialists read the fig tree as a lesson about watchfulness.
When the Bible uses the fig tree for Israel, is it a sign of blessing or of judgment?
In the Gospels it is almost always a sign of judgment. The fulfilled reading says that, if the fig tree is Israel, the image points to the fall of Jerusalem, not to a rebirth.

Lindsey wrote that the fig tree has been a historic symbol of Israel. The fulfilled reading asks how the Bible itself uses that symbol. In the prophets a fig tree can show blessing, as in "every man under his fig tree" (Micah 4:4). But when God judges Israel, he strikes its figs (Hosea 2:12; Joel 1:7; Jeremiah 8:13). Jeremiah saw good figs and bad figs (Jeremiah 24:1-10). In the Gospels, every fig tree tied to Israel is a picture of judgment. Jesus cursed a leafy tree with no fruit (Mark 11:12-14). He told a parable of a barren fig tree to be cut down (Luke 13:6-9). Read this way, a Jesus who used the fig tree for Israel was warning of judgment in that generation.
Jeremiah 8:13: "no figs on the fig tree" is a picture of judgment.
Luke 13:7: "Cut it down. Why should it use up the ground?" (paraphrase).

Futurists answer that judgment and later restoration often go together in the prophets (Hosea 3:4-5; Romans 11:25-26). They say the fig tree's judgment does not cancel a future blessing for Israel. Many amillennialists and postmillennialists also expect a future turning of many Jewish people to Christ, without linking it to a state.
Does the New Testament predict Israel's return to the land and a rebuilt temple?
The fulfilled reading finds no such prediction. The New Testament speaks of Jerusalem's coming destruction, but not of a later national restoration or third temple.

The Old Testament clearly predicted a return from exile. Jeremiah said it would happen after seventy years for Babylon (Jeremiah 29:10, 14). Daniel read that promise (Daniel 9:2). The return came under Cyrus from 538 BC, and the temple was rebuilt by 515 BC (Ezra 6:15). Isaiah spoke of a "second time" God would gather his people (Isaiah 11:11). The first time was the exodus from Egypt (Isaiah 11:16). On the fulfilled reading, the second time was the return from Babylon and Assyria. No third gathering is named. The New Testament speaks often of the temple's fall (Matthew 24:2; Luke 21:20-24). But it never says, "after this a temple will be rebuilt". Read this way, a teaching this central would surely be stated plainly, if it were true.
Ezra 1:1-3: Cyrus's decree in 538 BC fulfilled Jeremiah's seventy years.
John 2:20: the second temple, rebuilt and enlarged by Herod, had been "forty-six years" in building.

Futurists answer that Luke 21:24 implies an end to Gentile control of Jerusalem. They read Romans 11:26 and Acts 1:6-7 as expecting a restored Israel. They hold that Ezekiel 36-37 and Isaiah 11:11-12 ("from the four corners of the earth") go beyond the return from Babylon, since that return was small and from the east.
Was God's land promise to Israel already fulfilled?
Joshua says it was: God gave all the land he swore, and not one good promise failed. The fulfilled reading therefore sees no unfinished land promise awaiting the end.

Joshua 21:43-45 says the LORD gave Israel all the land he had sworn to their fathers. They took it and lived in it. Not one of his good promises failed; all came to pass. Joshua repeats this before he dies (Joshua 23:14). Nehemiah praises God for keeping his word to Abraham (Nehemiah 9:8). Under Solomon, Israel's rule reached the river Euphrates (1 Kings 4:21). Some futurist scholars reply that the borders of Numbers 34 were not reached, citing Joshua 13:1-7. On the fulfilled reading, Joshua 13 and Judges 3 speak of land still to be possessed by each tribe. The gift was given; the people's obedience lagged. Read this way, God kept his land promise in full. Later the New Testament widens the inheritance to the whole world (Romans 4:13).
1 Kings 4:21: Solomon ruled "from the river to the land of the Philistines".
Romans 4:13: Abraham's heirs will inherit "the world", not only Canaan.

Many futurist scholars say the land promise was eternal (Genesis 17:8) and only partly fulfilled. They point to later promises of return made after Joshua's day (Amos 9:14-15). They expect a final, permanent possession in the millennium. Covenant theologians agree the land was given, but see its fullness in the new creation.
Why did Jesus curse the fig tree, and how is it linked to the temple?
Mark places the curse around the temple scene. On the fulfilled reading, the leafy tree with no fruit pictures the temple system: impressive outside, but fruitless, and so under judgment.

Mark tells the story in three steps. Jesus enters the temple and looks around (Mark 11:11). The next morning he sees a fig tree in leaf, finds no fruit, and curses it (Mark 11:13-14). He then drives out the traders from the temple (Mark 11:15-17). The next day the disciples see the tree withered from the roots (Mark 11:20). On the fulfilled reading, the two stories explain each other. The temple had leaves: a grand building and busy worship. But it lacked the fruit of repentance that John the Baptist had demanded (Matthew 3:8-10). The leaders began seeking to destroy Jesus (Mark 11:18). Read this way, the curse was an acted prophecy. The temple would fall within a generation, as Jesus said soon after (Mark 13:2).
Mark 11:13: "it was not the season for figs". The lesson is about outward show, not the tree.
Isaiah 5:1-7: God looked for good grapes in his vineyard and found wild ones, so he judged it.

Most scholars of all views agree that the cursed fig tree is linked to the temple's judgment. Futurists accept this but say it pictures a judgment on that generation, not a final rejection of Israel. Many point to Romans 11:23-24, where branches cut off can be grafted in again.
What does the parable of the barren fig tree (Luke 13:6-9) teach?
A tree that bore nothing for three years was given one more season, then cut down if still fruitless. The fulfilled reading sees Jerusalem's final period of grace before AD 70.

A man came for three years looking for fruit on his fig tree and found none. He said, "Cut it down." The vinedresser asked for one more year to dig and feed it. If it still bore no fruit, it would be cut down (Luke 13:6-9). On the fulfilled reading, the parable fits Jesus' ministry to Israel. Just before this, Jesus warned, "unless you repent, you will all likewise perish" (Luke 13:3-5). Soon after, he wept over Jerusalem. He said enemies would surround it and leave not one stone on another, "because you did not know the time of your visitation" (Luke 19:41-44). Read this way, the tree pictures a nation given extra time, then judged when the time ran out.
Luke 13:4-5: those killed by the tower of Siloam are a warning to repent.
Luke 19:43-44: siege banks, encirclement and ruin, fulfilled when Titus besieged Jerusalem in AD 70 (Josephus, Jewish War 5.12.2).

Many interpreters of all schools agree that the parable warns Israel of coming judgment. Some reject linking the three years exactly to Jesus' ministry. Futurists add that the judgment of that generation does not end God's future plan for the Jewish people (Romans 11:1-2, 28-29).
Does Matthew 24:32 say the fig tree bears fruit or blossoms again?
No. Jesus speaks only of a tender branch and leaves. The fulfilled reading notes that leaves without fruit were exactly what Jesus cursed days earlier.

Some writers say Jesus called the cursed tree to mind and said, "watch it; when it blossoms again, all these things will happen". An older writer spoke of the tree putting out buds. On the fulfilled reading, the text says neither. Matthew 24:32 mentions only a tender branch and leaves. It says nothing of fruit, blossom or new life after death. And days before, Jesus had said to a fig tree, "Let no fruit grow on you ever again" (Matthew 21:19). Read this way, the futurist reading has Jesus contradict his own curse. The fulfilled reading sees no contradiction. The leaves of Matthew 24:32 are simply spring leaves, a sign that summer is near. The fruitless tree of Matthew 21 is a separate picture of judgment.
